title: Spill The T+1: Why Global Payment Playbooks Fail in Southeast Asia
summary: Xendit leaders share why global payment playbooks fail in Southeast Asia and how to choose a partner that won't leave you exposed. The post Spill The T+1: Why Global Payment Playbooks Fail in Southeast Asia appeared first on Xendit .
body_markdown:
Global merchants often bring their home-market playbook to Southeast Asia, and in a region this fragmented, it rarely holds up. In this episode of


*Spill the T+1* , **Alicia Vasquez** , Head of GTM USA, and **Tracy Prandi-Yuen** , Global Head of Account Management, draw on their years on the merchant side to explain where that playbook breaks down, and why the real test of a payments partner is what sits beneath the surface.


They cover:


- Why merchants still treating payments as a cost center are falling behind those using it to grow revenue.


- How the shift from e-wallets to real-time bank payments makes multiple direct bank connections essential.


- Why Southeast Asia is now a serious market for US businesses, and why their competitors are already moving in.


- The risk of picking a big global name that enters local markets shallowly and can't solve problems on the ground with banks and regulators.


- What merchants give up in transparency and compliance when their provider doesn't process payments or hold direct licenses itself.


## **Finding the Right Payments Partner**


**Tracy:** So you came from Pinterest, I came from Meta. I'm sure both of us have seen a lot of things that we wish we didn't see, or just things that, you know, we wish we'd known better, sooner, right? Like, I think many merchants kind of live through what we live through, and love to hear from your side. What have you seen on Pinterest side?


**Alicia:** One of the trends that I think merchants sometimes, particularly if I'm putting my Pinterest hat on, is not understanding that payments has evolved. It's no longer a cost center. Even if I think about, I used to report to the CFO org, you know, cost can be king, but now we're moving toward a world where it's a revenue center. And the players that really understand that, merchants that really understand that, are going to be ahead of the game.


So finding the right partner that can be that partner that helps you, you know, with embedded finance and other tools, can really step up your game. And you're going to your CFO, you're going with a revenue focus, and that's where the industry is going. So one of the things that I wish I knew earlier was that, is once I did, it changed the game for me. You know, I'm coming up with initiatives that is way beyond in a new playbook. So, yeah, that's my advice. Like, really look at your strategy and saying, "Okay, is this really just a cost play? Or can I optimize in different ways that does bring in that revenue for my business line?"


**Tracy:** Yeah, no, that makes so much sense. I've seen so many companies that just make decision of not even trying to expand outside of their Western markets, because they are already assumed that it's too hard for them to do it themselves. And that the providers they talk to may have painted a picture that refrained them from even making a move.


**Alicia** :


Right. And just share a little bit more about you. I know you have the Meta thing, what you're thinking on that.


**Tracy:** Yeah, while I was on Meta, you know, towards the end, I was really actively building redundancy and asking my partners if they were building redundancy. Because Meta had its days, right, where I've seen providers that just didn't work out from Meta. It could be financial troubles. It could be regulatory trouble.


And, you know, when you work for a really big company, one of the most important thing is to make sure that your company name, when it's in the headline, it's done in a positive way, right? So optics is extremely, extremely important in the way that the merchant manages it. There are always moments where certain partners may need to be put on pause or terminated in short notice, right?


And so I have seen days where we've had to just quickly compromise on taking on a new partner without doing enough homework, because we didn't have redundancy and we didn't have time. And so I think that was a big lesson that I learned in earlier days of Meta, and also seeing how my predecessors have done it. And so second half of my career there, that's what I focus on.


## **Evaluating Payment Connections in SEA**


**Tracy** :


The other thing is, you know, thinking about now, as we see in Southeast Asia, the user behavior, payment behavior, has slowly shifted from the user behavior from e-wallet focus to looking at real-time payments QR, right? That's starting to becoming more prominent than e-wallets, right? And that alone, I think, I would highly advise merchants now to really question their partners: "Are you, my partner, yourself building redundancy?"


Because in the past, you may offer an e-wallet and there's only one path there if you want a direct connection, right? But now you're doing bank payments. There's so many banks in every country. And if you're working with a partner that just goes into the country and do a light touch, right, they may connect shallow. Yeah, the better ones, they will go and connect to a bank, but it would be one thing. Maybe two, if they realize the first bank doesn't work really well, right? But some may just go straight to a local provider like Xendit, right?


But given how prominent now real-time payments is in Southeast Asia, it's very important to make sure whoever partner they connect with is not only having direct connections, but having a good network of banks that they're connecting directly to, so that there's redundancy. If something goes wrong, they have other paths. And that's so important, because when we think about infrastructure, internet, right, telecommunications in Southeast Asia, it's not always performing at its optimal level, right? And yeah, so things could get dropped so easily if you rely on only one or two bank connections.
